examples: A pride of lions was resting under the tree.
The pride is led by two related males.
Both prides hunt the same territory.
A young male leaves the pride at three.
Researchers have tracked this pride for a decade.

senses.head: The group of lions
examples: A pride of lions was resting under the tree.
The pride is led by two related males.
Both prides hunt the same territory.
A young male leaves the pride at three.
Researchers have tracked this pride for a decade.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the pride is hunting
entries.contrast: Used only of lions. The unrelated abstract noun pride, meaning self-respect, is uncountable.

examples: A murder of crows settled on the wires.
The murder is roosting in the same trees each night.
Both murders took off at once.
A murder of crows can strip a field fast.
The collective noun for crows is a murder.

senses.head: The group of crows
examples: A murder of crows settled on the wires.
The murder is roosting in the same trees each night.
Both murders took off at once.
A murder of crows can strip a field fast.
The collective noun for crows is a murder.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the murder is roosting
entries.contrast: The most famous of the ornamental terms, and used only of crows. Homonymous with the ordinary noun murder, a killing.

entries.meaning: A group of geese on the ground.
examples: A gaggle of geese blocked the whole path.
The gaggle is grazing on the fairway.
In flight they are a skein, not a gaggle.
A gaggle of reporters waited outside.
Both gaggles of tourists arrived at once.

senses.head: The group of geese
examples: A gaggle of geese blocked the whole path.
The gaggle is grazing on the fairway.
In flight they are a skein, not a gaggle.

senses.head: A noisy group of people
examples: A gaggle of reporters waited outside.
Both gaggles of tourists arrived at once.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the gaggle is blocking the path
entries.contrast: Strictly, gaggle is for geese on the ground; in flight they are a skein or a wedge. Also used jokingly of any noisy disorganized group of people.

entries.meaning: A group of whales, dolphins, or seals.
examples: A pod of dolphins followed the boat.
The pod is migrating north.
Both pods were tagged for tracking.
A resident pod returns to this inlet each year.
Orcas travel in matrilineal pods.

senses.head: The group of marine mammals
examples: A pod of dolphins followed the boat.
The pod is migrating north.
Both pods were tagged for tracking.
A resident pod returns to this inlet each year.
Orcas travel in matrilineal pods.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the pod is migrating
entries.counted with: a pod of whales, a pod of dolphins
entries.contrast: Used of marine mammals — whales, dolphins, seals. Also an ordinary noun meaning a seed case, and now a workspace or a small group of people.

entries.meaning: A group of monkeys or baboons.
examples: A troop of baboons crossed the road.
The troop is foraging along the riverbank.
Both troops avoid each other's range.
A troop may contain a hundred animals.
The dominant male leads the troop.

senses.head: The group of primates
examples: A troop of baboons crossed the road.
The troop is foraging along the riverbank.
Both troops avoid each other's range.
A troop may contain a hundred animals.
The dominant male leads the troop.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the troop is foraging
entries.counted with: a troop of monkeys, a troop of baboons
entries.contrast: Used of monkeys and baboons. Do not confuse with troupe, a group of performers, which is pronounced identically. The plural troops also means soldiers.

entries.meaning: A group of animals living together.
examples: A colony of ants had moved into the wall.
The bat colony is thriving again.
Both penguin colonies were counted from the air.
A single colony may contain millions of ants.
Bacterial colonies grew overnight on the plate.

senses.head: The group
examples: A colony of ants had moved into the wall.
The bat colony is thriving again.
Both penguin colonies were counted from the air.
A single colony may contain millions of ants.
Bacterial colonies grew overnight on the plate.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the colony is thriving
entries.counted with: a colony of ants, a colony of bats, a colony of penguins
entries.contrast: The broadest of the animal collectives, used for ants, bees, bats, penguins, seals, and bacteria alike. Also a political term.

entries.meaning: The young born to an animal at one birth.
examples: The litter is six weeks old now.
A litter of six puppies was born overnight.
Both litters came from the same mother.
She kept one kitten from the litter.
The runt of the litter needed hand feeding.

senses.head: The offspring
examples: The litter is six weeks old now.
A litter of six puppies was born overnight.
Both litters came from the same mother.
She kept one kitten from the litter.
The runt of the litter needed hand feeding.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the litter is six weeks old
entries.counted with: a litter of puppies, a litter of kittens
entries.contrast: Specifically the young born at one time to one mother. Also an uncountable noun meaning trash — don't drop litter — and cat litter.

entries.meaning: The young birds hatched at one time.
examples: The brood is nearly ready to fledge.
A brood of ducklings followed her across the road.
Both broods hatched the same week.
The hen kept her brood under the hedge.
He arrived with his entire brood.

senses.head: The hatchlings
examples: The brood is nearly ready to fledge.
A brood of ducklings followed her across the road.
Both broods hatched the same week.
The hen kept her brood under the hedge.

senses.head: Someone's children
examples: He arrived with his entire brood.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the brood is fledging
entries.contrast: Used of birds hatched at one time. Also a verb meaning to worry at length, and a jokey word for someone's children.

entries.meaning: A group of eggs laid at one time.
examples: The clutch is incubating under the female.
A clutch of four eggs is typical.
Both clutches failed that season.
She lays a second clutch if the first is lost.
The whole clutch hatched within a day.

senses.head: The eggs
examples: The clutch is incubating under the female.
A clutch of four eggs is typical.
Both clutches failed that season.
She lays a second clutch if the first is lost.
The whole clutch hatched within a day.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the clutch is incubating
entries.contrast: A clutch is the eggs; a brood is the chicks that hatch from them. Also the pedal in a car and a small handbag.

entries.meaning: A small group of game birds.
examples: A covey of quail exploded out of the grass.
The covey is holding tight in the brush.
Both coveys used the same field.
A covey usually numbers ten to fifteen birds.
Hunters look for a covey near cover.

senses.head: The group of birds
examples: A covey of quail exploded out of the grass.
The covey is holding tight in the brush.
Both coveys used the same field.
A covey usually numbers ten to fifteen birds.
Hunters look for a covey near cover.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the covey is holding tight
entries.counted with: a covey of quail, a covey of partridge
entries.contrast: A hunting term, used of small game birds. Note the pronunciation: KUV-ee, rhyming with lovey, not ✗ KOH-vee.

entries.meaning: A group of swans or birds; also any sizable group.
examples: A bevy of swans drifted past.
The bevy is on the far side of the lake.
A bevy of lawyers filed into the room.
The film won a bevy of awards.
Both bevies of reporters were kept outside.

senses.head: A group of birds
examples: A bevy of swans drifted past.
The bevy is on the far side of the lake.

senses.head: A large group of anything
examples: A bevy of lawyers filed into the room.
The film won a bevy of awards.
Both bevies of reporters were kept outside.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the bevy is on the water
entries.counted with: a bevy of swans, a bevy of quail
entries.contrast: Used of swans and some game birds, but far commoner now in the figurative sense: a bevy of lawyers, a bevy of awards.

examples: A parliament of owls is an unlikely sight.
The parliament is roosting in the barn.
Owls rarely gather, so a parliament is mostly a figure of speech.
Both parliaments were photographed at dusk.
The term plays on owls as symbols of wisdom.

senses.head: The group of owls
examples: A parliament of owls is an unlikely sight.
The parliament is roosting in the barn.
Owls rarely gather, so a parliament is mostly a figure of speech.
Both parliaments were photographed at dusk.
The term plays on owls as symbols of wisdom.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the parliament is roosting
entries.contrast: Ornamental and delightful, used only of owls, and probably invented for the pun on wise birds sitting in council. Also the ordinary political noun.

examples: An exaltation of larks rose from the field.
The exaltation is named for their song flight.
Both exaltations were heard before they were seen.
Few phrases in English are as pleasing as an exaltation of larks.
The term is poetic rather than ornithological.

senses.head: The group of larks
examples: An exaltation of larks rose from the field.
The exaltation is named for their song flight.
Both exaltations were heard before they were seen.
Few phrases in English are as pleasing as an exaltation of larks.
The term is poetic rather than ornithological.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the exaltation is rising
entries.contrast: Used only of larks, and named for their soaring song flight. The best known of the purely poetic terms, thanks to James Lipton's book An Exaltation of Larks.

examples: A charm of goldfinches settled on the thistles.
The charm is feeding on the seed heads.
Both charms returned to the same garden.
The word probably meant their blended chatter.
A charm of finches is a genuine dictionary term.

senses.head: The group of finches
examples: A charm of goldfinches settled on the thistles.
The charm is feeding on the seed heads.
Both charms returned to the same garden.
The word probably meant their blended chatter.
A charm of finches is a genuine dictionary term.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the charm is feeding
entries.counted with: a charm of finches, a charm of goldfinches
entries.contrast: Probably from an old word meaning a blended noise, later reinterpreted as the ordinary charm. Used of finches.

examples: A kindle of kittens filled the basket.
The kindle is still nursing.
Both kindles were born the same week.
Most people simply say a litter of kittens.
The word comes from an old verb meaning to give birth.

senses.head: The group of kittens
examples: A kindle of kittens filled the basket.
The kindle is still nursing.
Both kindles were born the same week.
Most people simply say a litter of kittens.
The word comes from an old verb meaning to give birth.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the kindle is nursing
entries.contrast: From an old verb meaning to give birth, unrelated to kindle 'to light a fire'. Rare; most people say a litter of kittens.

examples: A clowder of cats lives behind the restaurant.
The clowder is fed by a neighbor every evening.
Both clowders were trapped and neutered.
The word is related to clutter.
Almost nobody says clowder out loud.

senses.head: The group of cats
examples: A clowder of cats lives behind the restaurant.
The clowder is fed by a neighbor every evening.
Both clowders were trapped and neutered.
The word is related to clutter.
Almost nobody says clowder out loud.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the clowder is fed daily
entries.contrast: A genuine dictionary word, related to clutter, and almost never heard in speech. A group of cats is what people actually say.

examples: A sleuth of bears gathered at the falls.
The sleuth is feeding on the salmon run.
Both sleuths dispersed by October.
Bears are solitary, so the word is seldom used.
The detective sense of sleuth came much later.

senses.head: The group of bears
examples: A sleuth of bears gathered at the falls.
The sleuth is feeding on the salmon run.
Both sleuths dispersed by October.
Bears are solitary, so the word is seldom used.
The detective sense of sleuth came much later.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the sleuth is feeding
entries.contrast: Unrelated to sleuth meaning detective, which came later from sleuth-hound, a tracking dog. Bears are mostly solitary, so the term is rarely needed.

examples: A crash of rhinos moved through the scrub.
The crash is grazing near the waterhole.
Both crashes are under armed guard.
A crash of white rhinos may number a dozen.
The plural of rhinoceros is rhinoceroses.

senses.head: The group of rhinos
examples: A crash of rhinos moved through the scrub.
The crash is grazing near the waterhole.
Both crashes are under armed guard.
A crash of white rhinos may number a dozen.
The plural of rhinoceros is rhinoceroses.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the crash is grazing
entries.contrast: Vividly appropriate and genuinely attested. Note that the plural of rhinoceros is rhinoceroses, not ✗ rhinoceri.

examples: A tower of giraffes stood against the horizon.
The tower is browsing on the acacias.
Both towers were counted in the survey.
A moving group is sometimes called a journey.
The name is obviously about their height.

senses.head: The group of giraffes
examples: A tower of giraffes stood against the horizon.
The tower is browsing on the acacias.
Both towers were counted in the survey.
A moving group is sometimes called a journey.
The name is obviously about their height.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the tower is browsing
entries.contrast: Used when the animals are standing; a moving group is sometimes called a journey of giraffes. Both terms are real.

examples: A dazzle of zebras crossed ahead of the truck.
The dazzle is moving off toward the river.
Both dazzles mixed with the wildebeest.
The stripes genuinely confuse predators in motion.
The group is also called a zeal of zebras.

senses.head: The group of zebras
examples: A dazzle of zebras crossed ahead of the truck.
The dazzle is moving off toward the river.
Both dazzles mixed with the wildebeest.
The stripes genuinely confuse predators in motion.
The group is also called a zeal of zebras.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the dazzle is moving off
entries.contrast: Named for the visual confusion the stripes create in a moving group — a real anti-predator effect. Also called a zeal of zebras.

examples: A bloat of hippos filled the shallows.
The bloat is submerged most of the day.
Both bloats share the same stretch of river.
Hippo groups are also called pods.
The plural of the animal is hippopotamuses.

senses.head: The group of hippos
examples: A bloat of hippos filled the shallows.
The bloat is submerged most of the day.
Both bloats share the same stretch of river.
Hippo groups are also called pods.
The plural of the animal is hippopotamuses.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the bloat is submerged
entries.contrast: Also called a pod or a raft of hippos. Note the plural of the animal is hippopotamuses — see hippopotamus.

examples: A shrewdness of apes moved through the canopy.
The shrewdness is foraging near the ridge.
Both shrewdnesses were habituated to researchers.
Most people simply say a group of apes.
The term dates from medieval hunting books.

senses.head: The group of apes
examples: A shrewdness of apes moved through the canopy.
The shrewdness is foraging near the ridge.
Both shrewdnesses were habituated to researchers.
Most people simply say a group of apes.
The term dates from medieval hunting books.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the shrewdness is foraging
entries.contrast: One of the purely ornamental terms. In practice people say a group of apes or, for monkeys, a troop.

examples: A business of ferrets tumbled out of the box.
The business is asleep for most of the day.
Both businesses were rehomed together.
The term probably comes from busyness.
Ferret owners genuinely use the word.

senses.head: The group of ferrets
examples: A business of ferrets tumbled out of the box.
The business is asleep for most of the day.
Both businesses were rehomed together.
The term probably comes from busyness.
Ferret owners genuinely use the word.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the business is asleep
entries.contrast: Probably a corruption of busyness, describing how ferrets behave. Do not confuse with the ordinary noun business.

examples: A skulk of foxes crossed the field at dusk.
The skulk is entirely nocturnal here.
Both skulks denned in the same bank.
Foxes are mostly solitary, so the word is rare.
A group is also called a leash of foxes.

senses.head: The group of foxes
examples: A skulk of foxes crossed the field at dusk.
The skulk is entirely nocturnal here.
Both skulks denned in the same bank.
Foxes are mostly solitary, so the word is rare.
A group is also called a leash of foxes.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the skulk is nocturnal
entries.contrast: From the verb skulk, to move furtively. Foxes are largely solitary, so the term is mostly ornamental. A group is also called a leash or an earth of foxes.

entries.meaning: A group of starlings, especially in swirling flight.
examples: A murmuration of starlings darkened the sky.
The murmuration is forming over the reeds.
Both murmurations merged into one.
A murmuration can contain a million birds.
The word names the sound of their wings.

senses.head: The group of starlings
examples: A murmuration of starlings darkened the sky.
The murmuration is forming over the reeds.
Both murmurations merged into one.
A murmuration can contain a million birds.
The word names the sound of their wings.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the murmuration is forming
entries.contrast: Unusually among the ornamental terms, this one is in genuine current use, because the swirling flight of starlings is a famous natural spectacle.

examples: An unkindness of ravens circled the tower.
The unkindness is nesting on the cliff face.
Both unkindnesses were counted at the roost.
Crows get a murder; ravens get an unkindness.
A group of ravens is also called a conspiracy.

senses.head: The group of ravens
examples: An unkindness of ravens circled the tower.
The unkindness is nesting on the cliff face.
Both unkindnesses were counted at the roost.
Crows get a murder; ravens get an unkindness.
A group of ravens is also called a conspiracy.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the unkindness is circling
entries.contrast: Ravens get an unkindness; crows get a murder. Both are medieval and both are ornamental.

examples: A mob of kangaroos grazed at the edge of the road.
The mob is resting in the shade.
Both mobs use the same waterhole.
An angry mob gathered outside.
Both mobs were dispersed by nightfall.

senses.head: The group of kangaroos
examples: A mob of kangaroos grazed at the edge of the road.
The mob is resting in the shade.
Both mobs use the same waterhole.

senses.head: A disorderly crowd
examples: An angry mob gathered outside.
Both mobs were dispersed by nightfall.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the mob is grazing
entries.contrast: This is the ordinary Australian word for a group of kangaroos, not an ornamental one. Also means a disorderly crowd of people, and organized crime.

entries.meaning: A group of animals floating on water.
examples: A raft of otters drifted past, holding hands.
The raft is sleeping anchored in the kelp.
Both rafts of ducks stayed near the bank.
The government announced a raft of new measures.
A raft of complaints followed the change.

senses.head: The floating group
examples: A raft of otters drifted past, holding hands.
The raft is sleeping anchored in the kelp.
Both rafts of ducks stayed near the bank.

senses.head: A large number of things
examples: The government announced a raft of new measures.
A raft of complaints followed the change.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the raft is drifting
entries.counted with: a raft of otters, a raft of ducks
entries.contrast: Used of animals floating together on water. Also very common figuratively: a raft of measures, a raft of complaints.

examples: A shiver of sharks circled the bait ball.
The shiver is feeding at the surface.
Both shivers were filmed from above.
A group of sharks is also called a school.
The name is deliberately unsettling.

senses.head: The group of sharks
examples: A shiver of sharks circled the bait ball.
The shiver is feeding at the surface.
Both shivers were filmed from above.
A group of sharks is also called a school.
The name is deliberately unsettling.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the shiver is circling
entries.contrast: Aptly named, and genuinely attested. Also the ordinary noun and verb meaning to tremble.

entries.meaning: A group of animals sharing a nest; also the structure itself.
examples: A nest of vipers was found under the shed.
The nest is dormant through the winter.
Both nests were relocated safely.
The department was a nest of intrigue.
He walked into a nest of vipers.

senses.head: The group
examples: A nest of vipers was found under the shed.
The nest is dormant through the winter.
Both nests were relocated safely.

senses.head: A treacherous group of people
examples: The department was a nest of intrigue.
He walked into a nest of vipers.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the nest is dormant
entries.counted with: a nest of vipers, a nest of ants
entries.contrast: Both the structure and the group inhabiting it. The figurative a nest of vipers, meaning a treacherous group of people, is very common.

entries.meaning: A group of toads; also a small tight group of people.
examples: A knot of toads gathered at the pond.
The knot is spawning in the shallows.
A knot of onlookers formed on the sidewalk.
Both knots of protesters were peaceful.
A knot of reporters blocked the door.

senses.head: The group of toads
examples: A knot of toads gathered at the pond.
The knot is spawning in the shallows.

senses.head: A small group of people
examples: A knot of onlookers formed on the sidewalk.
Both knots of protesters were peaceful.
A knot of reporters blocked the door.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the knot is spawning
entries.contrast: Also used of a small tight group of people — a knot of onlookers — which is far commoner than the toad sense.

entries.meaning: A group of frogs or caterpillars; also any large organized group.
examples: An army of frogs crossed the road after the rain.
The army of caterpillars stripped the tree bare.
An army of volunteers sorted the donations.
Both armies of lawyers billed by the hour.
He hired an army of consultants.

senses.head: The group of animals
examples: An army of frogs crossed the road after the rain.
The army of caterpillars stripped the tree bare.

senses.head: A large organized group of people
examples: An army of volunteers sorted the donations.
Both armies of lawyers billed by the hour.
He hired an army of consultants.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the army is on the move
entries.counted with: an army of frogs, an army of caterpillars
entries.contrast: Used of frogs and of caterpillars, and constantly figuratively of any large organized group: an army of volunteers.

entries.meaning: A group of locusts; also a widespread affliction.
examples: A plague of locusts destroyed the entire crop.
The plague is moving west across the region.
Both plagues were the worst in decades.
The neighborhood suffered a plague of break-ins.
It was the third plague of that century.

senses.head: The swarm of locusts
examples: A plague of locusts destroyed the entire crop.
The plague is moving west across the region.
Both plagues were the worst in decades.

senses.head: A widespread affliction
examples: The neighborhood suffered a plague of break-ins.
It was the third plague of that century.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the plague is moving west
entries.contrast: Used almost exclusively of locusts, with a strong biblical association. Also the disease, and a figurative sense: a plague of burglaries.

entries.meaning: A group of animals being driven along.
examples: A drove of cattle blocked the lane.
The drove is being moved to summer pasture.
Both droves took the old road.
Voters turned out in droves.
They left the city in droves that summer.

senses.head: The moving group
examples: A drove of cattle blocked the lane.
The drove is being moved to summer pasture.
Both droves took the old road.

senses.head: Large numbers of people
examples: Voters turned out in droves.
They left the city in droves that summer.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the drove is on the move
entries.counted with: a drove of cattle, a drove of pigs
entries.contrast: Specifically animals being driven somewhere, as opposed to a herd simply standing. The plural droves means large numbers of people: they came in droves.

entries.meaning: A group of wolves or dogs.
examples: A pack of wolves brought down the elk.
The pack is hunting at the edge of the range.
Both packs defend separate territories.
A pack is usually one family group.
He broke away from the pack on the last climb.

senses.head: The group of canines
examples: A pack of wolves brought down the elk.
The pack is hunting at the edge of the range.
Both packs defend separate territories.
A pack is usually one family group.

senses.head: A group of cyclists or runners
examples: He broke away from the pack on the last climb.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the pack is hunting
entries.counted with: a pack of wolves, a pack of dogs
entries.contrast: Used of wolves, dogs, and hounds. Also the container sense — see pack — and a group of cyclists in a race.
